claim: ABIG1 is required for abscisic acid (ABA) mediated growth inhibition
source: Here we identify a transcription factor, ABA INSENSITIVE GROWTH 1 (ABIG1) required for abscisic acid (ABA) mediated growth inhibition, but not for stomatal closure.
evidence: Demonstrated through loss-of-function mutant experiments showing abig1 mutants remain greener and produce more leaves than wild-type when treated with ABA

claim: ABIG1 is not required for stomatal closure
source: Here we identify a transcription factor, ABA INSENSITIVE GROWTH 1 (ABIG1) required for abscisic acid (ABA) mediated growth inhibition, but not for stomatal closure.
evidence: Shown through stomatal closure assays where abig1-1 mutants showed similar stomatal closure response to ABA as wild-type

claim: ABIG1 mRNA levels increase in response to drought
source: ABIG1 mRNA levels are increased both in response to drought and in response to ABA treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by Q-RTPCR measurements showing ABIG1 mRNA increases with decreasing soil moisture

claim: ABIG1 mRNA levels increase in response to ABA treatment
source: ABIG1 mRNA levels are increased both in response to drought and in response to ABA treatment.
evidence: Shown by Q-RTPCR experiments on liquid grown seedlings treated with ABA

claim: abig1 mutants remain greener when treated with ABA compared to wild-type plants
source: When treated with ABA, abig1 mutants remain greener and produce more leaves than comparable wild-type plants.
evidence: Demonstrated through visual observation and chlorophyll measurements in ABA treatment experiments

claim: abig1 mutants produce more leaves than wild-type when treated with ABA
source: When treated with ABA, abig1 mutants remain greener and produce more leaves than comparable wild-type plants.
evidence: Shown through leaf number counts in ABA treatment experiments

claim: abig1 mutants have fewer yellow, senesced leaves than wild-type when challenged with drought
source: When challenged with drought, abig1 mutants have fewer yellow, senesced leaves than wild-type.
evidence: Demonstrated through drought experiments where water was withheld and percentage of yellow leaves was measured

claim: Induction of ABIG1 transcription mimics ABA treatment
source: Induction of ABIG1 transcription mimics ABA treatment and regulates a set of genes implicated in stress responses.
evidence: Shown through estradiol-inducible overexpression experiments where ABIG1 induction caused similar phenotypes to ABA application

claim: ABIG1 regulates a set of genes implicated in stress responses
source: Induction of ABIG1 transcription mimics ABA treatment and regulates a set of genes implicated in stress responses.
evidence: Demonstrated through RNA-seq experiments identifying genes differentially expressed upon ABIG1 induction

claim: Drought acts through ABA to increase ABIG1 transcription
source: We propose a model in which drought acts through ABA to increase ABIG1 transcription which in turn restricts new shoot growth and promotes leaf senescence.
evidence: Supported by observations that both drought and ABA increase ABIG1 mRNA levels, and that this response is partially dependent on ABI1

claim: ABIG1 restricts new shoot growth
source: We propose a model in which drought acts through ABA to increase ABIG1 transcription which in turn restricts new shoot growth and promotes leaf senescence.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing abig1 mutants produce more leaves and have longer petioles when treated with ABA, and overexpression causes growth inhibition

claim: ABIG1 promotes leaf senescence
source: We propose a model in which drought acts through ABA to increase ABIG1 transcription which in turn restricts new shoot growth and promotes leaf senescence.
evidence: Shown through drought experiments where abig1 mutants had fewer yellow leaves and higher chlorophyll content, and overexpression caused leaf yellowing

claim: Drought inhibits plant growth
source: Drought inhibits plant growth and can also induce premature senescence.
evidence: Established fact in plant biology supported by cited literature

claim: Drought can induce premature senescence
source: Drought inhibits plant growth and can also induce premature senescence.
evidence: Established fact in plant biology supported by cited literature

claim: Plants slow or stop new growth to withstand drought, thereby conserving resources
source: One way for plants to withstand drought is to slow, or stop, new growth thereby conserving resources until better times return (Dolferus, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dolferus, 2014

claim: Growth arrest coincides with predictable dry periods during the life cycle such as in seed development or seasonal bud dormancy
source: Growth arrest coincides with predictable dry periods during the life cycle – such as in seed development or seasonal bud dormancy.
evidence: Established knowledge in plant biology

claim: Growth arrest or reduction can occur in response to sporadic drought
source: Growth arrest or reduction can also occur in response to sporadic drought (e.g. Marc and Palmer, 1976; Verelst et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Marc and Palmer, 1976 and Verelst et al., 2013

claim: Drought induced leaf senescence allows the plant to recover nutrients and reduce the water cost of maintaining the leaf
source: More extreme than growth arrest is a response in which parts of the plant are sacrificed, as for instance in drought induced leaf senescence, allowing the plant to recover nutrients and to reduce the water cost of maintaining the leaf (Munné-Bosch et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munné-Bosch et al., 2004

claim: ABA is the best known plant hormone for its ability to allow plants to withstand drought
source: Among plant hormones, abscisic acid (ABA) is the best known for its ability to allow plants to withstand drought.
evidence: Established knowledge in plant biology

claim: Levels of the ABA biosynthetic enzyme AtNCED3 increase in the vascular parenchyma in response to desiccation in Arabidopsis
source: In response to desiccation, levels of the ABA biosynthetic enzyme AtNCED3 in the vascular parenchyma increase in Arabidopsis (Endo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Endo et al., 2008

claim: Increased ABA causes plants to close stomatal apertures, thus reducing water loss
source: This causes an increase in ABA which causes plants to close stomatal apertures, thus reducing water loss (Schroeder et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schroeder et al., 2001

claim: Increases in ABA concentration during seed development impose maturation and dormancy on seeds
source: Increases in ABA concentration during seed development impose maturation and dormancy on seeds (Finkelstein, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finkelstein, 2013

claim: ABA acts by binding to PYR-like co-receptors and bringing them together with PP2C family phosphatases
source: ABA acts by binding to PYR-like co-receptors and bringing them together with PP2C family phosphatases (Cutler et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cutler et al., 2010

claim: ABA binding frees downstream SNRK2 kinases from repression by the PP2C phosphatase
source: This frees downstream SNRK2 kinases from repression by the PP2C phosphatase, allowing the kinase to modify protein targets at the plasma membrane - to alter turgor in guard cells - or to modify a set of transcription factors - to promote maturation and dormancy in the developing seed.
evidence: Established mechanism of ABA signaling

claim: Exogenously applied ABA slows growth of roots and shoots
source: Exogenously applied ABA slows growth of roots and shoots: it promotes dormancy in axillary buds (Shimizu-Sato and Mori, 2001), inhibits formation and growth of leaves (Marc and Palmer, 1976; Verelst et al., 2013) and inhibits root growth (DeSmet et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: ABA promotes dormancy in axillary buds
source: Exogenously applied ABA slows growth of roots and shoots: it promotes dormancy in axillary buds (Shimizu-Sato and Mori, 2001), inhibits formation and growth of leaves (Marc and Palmer, 1976; Verelst et al., 2013) and inhibits root growth (DeSmet et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shimizu-Sato and Mori, 2001

claim: ABA inhibits formation and growth of leaves
source: Exogenously applied ABA slows growth of roots and shoots: it promotes dormancy in axillary buds (Shimizu-Sato and Mori, 2001), inhibits formation and growth of leaves (Marc and Palmer, 1976; Verelst et al., 2013) and inhibits root growth (DeSmet et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marc and Palmer, 1976 and Verelst et al., 2013

claim: ABA inhibits root growth
source: Exogenously applied ABA slows growth of roots and shoots: it promotes dormancy in axillary buds (Shimizu-Sato and Mori, 2001), inhibits formation and growth of leaves (Marc and Palmer, 1976; Verelst et al., 2013) and inhibits root growth (DeSmet et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeSmet et al., 2003

claim: ABA can promote drought induced leaf senescence
source: ABA also can promote drought induced leaf senescence (Munné-Bosch and Alegre, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munné-Bosch and Alegre, 2004

claim: ABA biosynthetic mutants with reduced levels of ABA are smaller than wild type plants
source: This conclusion is based on the observation that biosynthetic mutants with reduced levels of ABA are smaller than wild type plants (Barrero et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrero et al., 2005

claim: Supplementation with ABA restores growth of ABA biosynthetic mutants grown under well watered conditions
source: Supplementation with ABA restores growth of plants grown under well watered conditions indicating the growth defect is not a secondary consequence of water loss.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations on ABA biosynthetic mutants

claim: REVOLUTA and KANADI1 oppositely control components of the ABA signaling pathway
source: REVOLUTA (REV) and KANADI1 (KAN1), opposing regulators of leaf polarity and meristem formation, also oppositely control components of the ABA signaling pathway (Reinhart et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhart et al., 2013

claim: ABA signaling genes are prominent among the ORK genes (genes oppositely regulated by the REV and KAN transcription factors)
source: since ABA signaling genes are prominent among the small set of ORK genes (genes oppositely regulated by the REV and KAN transcription factors (Reinhart et al., 2013; Figure 1A)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A and supported by citation to Reinhart et al., 2013

claim: The set of eight ORK genes includes PYL6 and CIPK12, two genes involved in ABA signaling
source: The set of eight ORK genes (OPPOSITELY REGULATED BY REVOLUTA AND KANADI) includes two genes involved in ABA signaling: PYL6 and CIPK12.
evidence: Stated as fact with supporting references for PYL6 and CIPK12 functions

claim: PYL6 encodes a member of the family of ABA receptors
source: PYL6 encodes a member of the family of ABA receptors (Park et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2009

claim: CIPK12 encodes a member of a family of SNRK3 kinases that play a role in the ABA regulatory pathway
source: CIPK12 encodes a member of a family of SNRK3 kinases that play a role in the ABA regulatory pathway (Qin et al., 2008; Lumba et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Qin et al., 2008 and Lumba et al., 2014

claim: ZFP8 plays a role in trichome development
source: Except forZFP8, which plays a role in trichome development (Gan et al., 2007), the function of the other five genes at this regulatory node is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gan et al., 2007

claim: HAT22 is one of 10 Class II HOMEODOMAIN-LEUCINE ZIPPER (HD-ZIPII) genes
source: HAT22 is one of 10 Class II HOMEODOMAIN-LEUCINE ZIPPER (HD-ZIPII) genes (Ciarbelli et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ciarbelli et al., 2008

claim: ABIG1 mRNA levels increase in liquid grown seedlings treated with ABA
source: ABIG1 mRNA levels increase in liquid grown seedlings treated with ABA (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Q-RTPCR data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: ABIG1 mRNA levels did not increase in homozygous abig1-1 mutants treated with ABA
source: ABIG1 mRNA levels did not increase in homozygous abig1-1 mutants treated with ABA (Figure 1C), presumably because the inserted DS element causes transcript termination early in the ABIG1 transcript.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C with inference about mechanism

claim: The increase in ABIG1 mRNA is reduced in ABA treated abi1 mutant seedlings
source: The increase in ABIG1 mRNA is reduced in ABA treated abi1 mutant seedlings defective for the ABI1 PP2C protein phosphatase, a co-receptor for ABA (p (treatment by genotype) = 0.0033, 2 way ANOVA; Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Q-RTPCR data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: ABA stimulation of ABIG1 mRNA increase utilizes, at least in part, the core ABA signaling pathway
source: Thus, ABA stimulation of ABIG1 mRNA increase utilizes, at least in part, the core ABA signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that abi1 mutants show reduced ABIG1 response to ABA

claim: ABIG1 mRNA levels increase with decreasing soil moisture
source: Indeed, ABIG1 mRNA levels increase with decreasing soil moisture (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Q-RTPCR measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: ABIG1/HAT22 mRNA is up-regulated in flowers in response to drought
source: The response of ABIG1 expression to drought has also been noted by Su et al. (2013) who found ABIG1/HAT22 mRNA up-regulated in flowers in response to drought.
evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 2013

claim: The abig1-1/GT7363 line carries an engineered DS transposable element inserted into the sixth codon of the ABIG1 coding sequence
source: The abig1-1/ GT7363 line carries an engineered DS transposable element inserted into the sixth codon of the ABIG1 coding sequence (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B

claim: In abig1-1/+ plants, GUS is expressed in cells surrounding the vascular strand with highest levels in the petioles, the hypocotyl and subtending the shoot apical meristem and youngest leaf primordia
source: In abig1-1/+ plants, GUS is expressed in cells surrounding the vascular strand with highest levels in the petioles, the hypocotyl and subtending the shoot apical meristem and youngest leaf primordia (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by GUS staining patterns shown in Figure 1G-I

claim: GUS expression in the petiole is highest in the vascular parenchyma associated with the tracheary elements of the xylem
source: Cross sections show GUS expression in the petiole to be highest in the vascular parenchyma associated with the tracheary elements of the xylem.
evidence: Observed in histological cross sections

claim: Transfer of heterozygous abig1/+ plants to solid media containing 5 microMolar ABA resulted in an increase in the intensity and extent of GUS expression
source: Consistent with the Q-RTPCR measurements above, the transfer of heterozygous abig1/+ plants to solid media containing 5 microMolar ABA resulted in an increase in the intensity and extent of GUS expression (Figure 1F,K).
evidence: Demonstrated by GUS staining shown in Figure 1F and K

claim: Exogenously added ABA travels upward from the root toward the shoot
source: These patterns of expression are consistent with observations showing exogenously added ABA traveling upward from the root toward the shoot (Waadt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waadt et al., 2014

claim: The location of ABIG1/HAT22 mRNA expression in the vascular parenchyma is consistent with the location of increased ABA biosynthetic enzymes in response to drought
source: The location of ABIG1/HAT22 mRNA expression in the vascular parenchyma is also consistent with the location of increased ABA biosynthetic enzymes in response to drought (Endo et al., 2008).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with cited literature

claim: HD-ZIPII proteins bind to their own promoters and negatively regulate their own transcription
source: HD-ZIPII proteins are known to bind to their own promoters and negatively regulate their own transcription (Ciarbelli et al., 2008; Turchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ciarbelli et al., 2008 and Turchi et al., 2013

claim: Homozygous abig1-1 plants show higher and more expanded GUS expression than heterozygotes
source: Indeed, homozygous abig1-1 plants show higher and more expanded GUS expression than heterozygotes (compare Figure 1J to Figure 1L).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing GUS staining patterns in Figure 1J and 1L

claim: ABA treatment did not increase the already high levels of reporter expression seen in abig1-1 homozygotes
source: ABA treatment did not increase the already high levels of reporter expression seen in abig1-1 homozygotes. (Figure 1L,M).
evidence: Shown by GUS staining in Figure 1L and M

claim: ABA acts indirectly to increase ABIG1 levels by interfering with the negative autoregulatory action of the ABIG1 protein
source: This suggests that ABA acts indirectly to increase ABIG1 levels by interfering with the negative autoregulatory action of the ABIG1 protein.
evidence: Inferred from observations of GUS expression patterns in heterozygotes vs homozygotes with and without ABA

claim: There are no ABREs (ABA Response elements) in the 1000 bp upstream of ABIG1
source: This is an attractive hypothesis given the absence of ABREs (ABA Response elements) in the 1000 bp upstream of ABIG1.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of ABIG1 promoter region

claim: abig1-1 mutant seeds germinate similarly to wild type seeds in their inability to germinate in the presence of ABA
source: In contrast to canonical ABA insensitive (abi) mutants (Koorneef et al., 1984; Finkelstein, 1994), abig1-1 mutants were similar to wild type seeds in their inability to germinate in the presence of ABA, a potent germination inhibitor (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by germination assays shown in Figure 2A

claim: ABA applied to the epidermis of wild-type and abig1-1 mutant leaves caused similar decreases in stomatal apertures
source: ABA applied to the epidermis of wild-type and abig1-1 mutant leaves caused similar decreases in stomatal apertures (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by stomatal closure measurements shown in Figure 2B

claim: ABA inhibited growth and caused leaf yellowing in wild type seedlings
source: Under this treatment regimen ABA inhibited growth and caused leaf yellowing in wild type seedlings (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3

claim: ABA caused fewer leaves to develop at the shoot apex and caused leaves to have shorter petioles and smaller leaf blades
source: ABA caused fewer leaves to develop at the shoot apex, and caused leaves to have shorter petioles and smaller leaf blades.
evidence: Observed in morphological measurements of ABA-treated plants

claim: abig1-1 mutants differed from wild-type in their response to ABA with regard to leaf number (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.0001)
source: abig1 mutants differed in their response to ABA with regard to leaf number (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.0001) and petiole length (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.02) but not root length (p(genotype by [ABA]) = 0.285) as determined using a 2 way ANOVA analysis.
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of morphological measurements

claim: abig1-1 mutants differed from wild-type in their response to ABA with regard to petiole length (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.02)
source: abig1 mutants differed in their response to ABA with regard to leaf number (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.0001) and petiole length (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.02) but not root length (p(genotype by [ABA]) = 0.285) as determined using a 2 way ANOVA analysis.
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of morphological measurements

claim: abig1-1 mutants did not differ from wild-type in their response to ABA with regard to root length (p(genotype by [ABA]) = 0.285)
source: abig1 mutants differed in their response to ABA with regard to leaf number (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.0001) and petiole length (p(genotype by [ABA]) <0.02) but not root length (p(genotype by [ABA]) = 0.285) as determined using a 2 way ANOVA analysis.
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analysis of morphological measurements

claim: Wild type ABIG1 function is required for ABA-mediated inhibition of leaf production and petiole growth
source: We conclude that the wild type ABIG1 function is required for ABA-mediated inhibition of leaf production and petiole growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that abig1 mutants show reduced response to ABA for these traits

claim: Induced overexpression of ABIG1 mimicked application of ABA to wild type plants
source: Induced overexpression of ABIG1 (achieved by placing the ABIG1 cDNA under the control of an estradiol inducible XVE transcription factor [Zuo et al., 2000]) mimicked application of ABA to wild type plants.
evidence: Demonstrated by phenotypic observations of XVE:ABIG1 plants treated with estradiol

claim: Overexpression of ABIG1 caused leaves to develop with small blades and short petioles, leaves to be yellow, and fewer leaves to be made
source: Leaves developed with small blades and short petioles, leaves were yellow, and fewer leaves were made (Figure 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4

claim: Increased ABIG1 mRNA levels are sufficient to cause growth inhibition and leaf yellowing
source: Thus, increased ABIG1 mRNA levels are sufficient to cause growth inhibition and leaf yellowing.
evidence: Inferred from overexpression experiments

claim: Köllmer et al. (2011) found a modest increase in leaf senescence when ABIG1 (HAT22) was expressed under control of the 35S promoter
source: We note that this is consistent with results by Köllmer et al. (2011) who found a modest increase in leaf senescence when ABIG1 (HAT22) was expressed under control of the 35S promoter.
evidence: Supported by citation to Köllmer et al., 2011

claim: Addition of increasing concentrations of ABA to estradiol treated XVE:ABIG1 plants did not make the phenotype more extreme than when estradiol alone was added
source: Addition of increasing concentrations of ABA to estradiol treated XVE:ABIG1 plants did not make the phenotype more extreme than when estradiol alone was added (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C-E

claim: The major role for ABA in regulating plant growth is through its role in promoting the ABIG1 transcript accumulation
source: This supports a model in which the major role for ABA in regulating plant growth is through its role in promoting the ABIG1 transcript accumulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that additional ABA does not enhance the phenotype of ABIG1 overexpression

claim: Under well-watered conditions, abig1-1 mutants had a lower percentage of yellow, senesced leaves than wild-type
source: Under well-watered conditions, abig1-1 mutants had a lower percentage of yellow, senesced leaves than wild-type (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5

claim: Chlorophyll content decreased significantly more in wild type than in the abig1-1 mutant
source: For one experimental replicate, the amount of chlorophyll present in leaves was measured (Figure 5G). It was found to decrease significantly more in the wild type than in the mutant.
evidence: Demonstrated by chlorophyll measurements shown in Figure 5G

claim: After 17 days of withholding water, the percent yellow or senesced leaves more than doubled in wild type but only increased modestly in homozygous abig1-1 mutant (p(treatment × genotype) = 0.0008)
source: After 17 days of withholding water, this difference became significantly more pronounced with the percent yellow or senesced leaves more than doubling in the wild type but only increasing modestly in the homozygous abig1-1 mutant (p(treatment × genotype) = 0.0008; Figure 5B,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by measurements shown in Figure 5B and D with statistical analysis

claim: Under water withheld conditions, wild type plants made fewer side branches than under well watered conditions while abig1 mutants continued to produce the same number of side branches (p(treatment × genotype) = 0.0114)
source: Under water withheld conditions, wild type plants made fewer side branches than under well watered conditions while abig1 mutants continued to produce the same number of side branches (p(treatment × genotype) = 0.0114; Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by branch counts shown in Figure 5E with statistical analysis

claim: Wild type plants were unable to remain upright under drought conditions while mutant plants remained erect
source: The wild type plants were unable to remain upright while the mutant plants remained erect (Figure 5B ; 100% erect mutant plants (n = 9) vs 37.5% erect wild type plants (n = 9) in one experiment with similar results in 3 additional replicated experiments).
evidence: Demonstrated by visual observation shown in Figure 5B with quantification

claim: Wild type plants showed less extensive root systems than the abig1-1 mutants under drought conditions
source: Wild type plants also showed less extensive root systems than the abig1-1 mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C

claim: The ABIG1 transcription factor accelerates leaf senescence
source: We conclude that the ABIG1 transcription factor accelerates leaf senescence and acts to prevent the plant from remaining erect under dry conditions.
evidence: Inferred from drought experiments showing abig1 mutants have fewer yellow leaves and remain greener

claim: ABIG1 acts to prevent the plant from remaining erect under dry conditions
source: We conclude that the ABIG1 transcription factor accelerates leaf senescence and acts to prevent the plant from remaining erect under dry conditions.
evidence: Inferred from drought experiments showing wild-type plants droop while abig1 mutants remain erect

claim: ABA resistant mutants isolated in the past have been associated with drought sensitivity rather than drought resistance
source: This result was unexpected since ABA resistant mutants isolated in the past have been associated with drought sensitivity rather than drought resistance (see e.g. Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2009

claim: 18 mRNAs are up-regulated in response to ABIG1 induction
source: The final list includes 18 up-regulated mRNAs (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1) and 14 down-regulated mRNAs (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Identified through RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: 14 mRNAs are down-regulated in response to ABIG1 induction
source: The final list includes 18 up-regulated mRNAs (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1) and 14 down-regulated mRNAs (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Identified through RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Down-regulated genes showed statistically significant over-representation for Gene Ontology (GO) terms associated with response to stress, response to abiotic or biotic stimulus, and signal transduction
source: Down-regulated, but not up-regulated, genes, showed statistically significant over-representation for Gene Ontology (GO) terms associated with response to stress, response to abiotic or biotic stimulus, and signal transduction (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: The EAR domain of ABIG1 interacts with the TOPLESS co-repressor
source: The interaction of the EAR domain of ABIG1 with the TOPLESS co-repressor (Causier et al., 2012; T. Liu and M.K.Barton, unpublished), and the demonstrated ability of HD-ZIPII factors to repress their own transcription (Ohgishi et al., 2001; Ciarbelli et al., 2008) are evidence that ABIG1 acts a repressor.
evidence: Supported by citation to Causier et al., 2012 and unpublished data

claim: HD-ZIPII factors can repress their own transcription
source: The interaction of the EAR domain of ABIG1 with the TOPLESS co-repressor (Causier et al., 2012; T. Liu and M.K.Barton, unpublished), and the demonstrated ability of HD-ZIPII factors to repress their own transcription (Ohgishi et al., 2001; Ciarbelli et al., 2008) are evidence that ABIG1 acts a repressor.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohgishi et al., 2001 and Ciarbelli et al., 2008

claim: ABIG1 acts as a repressor
source: The interaction of the EAR domain of ABIG1 with the TOPLESS co-repressor (Causier et al., 2012; T. Liu and M.K.Barton, unpublished), and the demonstrated ability of HD-ZIPII factors to repress their own transcription (Ohgishi et al., 2001; Ciarbelli et al., 2008) are evidence that ABIG1 acts a repressor.
evidence: Inferred from domain structure and known functions of similar proteins

claim: Direct targets of ABIG1 are expected to fall among the genes down-regulated by ABIG1 induction
source: Direct targets of ABIG1 are therefore expected to fall among the genes down-regulated by ABIG1 induction.
evidence: Inferred from the conclusion that ABIG1 acts as a repressor

claim: The promoters (500 bp upstream of the ATG) of the down regulated genes are enriched for bHLH, MADS and a homeodomain transcription factor binding sites
source: The promoters (500 bp upstream of the ATG) of the down regulated genes are enriched for bHLH, MADS and a homeodomain transcription factor binding sites (p=1.6E-4, p=1.5E-2 and p=1.9E-2 respectively; P-Scan (Zambelli et al., 2009)).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational analysis using P-Scan

claim: Promoters for up-regulated genes were enriched for bZIP transcription factor binding sites (p = 4.1E-3)
source: Promoters for up-regulated genes were enriched for bZIP transcription factor binding sites (p = 4.1E-3).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational analysis

claim: CYP707A3 encodes an enzyme that catabolizes ABA
source: Notable among the regulated genes are: CYP707A3 which encodes an enzyme that catabolizes ABA (Umezawa et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Umezawa et al., 2006

claim: GRF5 regulates leaf senescence and chloroplast number
source: GRF5 which regulates leaf senescence and chloroplast number (Vercruyssen et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vercruyssen et al., 2015

claim: ATHB5 is a gene implicated in drought resistance
source: ATHB5, a gene implicated in drought resistance (Johannesson et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Johannesson et al., 2003

claim: TOPLESS RELATED 3 (TPR3) is a member of the TOPLESS co-repressor gene family and a likely partner of the ABIG1 transcription factor
source: TOPLESS RELATED 3 (TPR3), a member of the TOPLESS co-repressor gene family and a likely partner of the ABIG1 transcription factor (Causier et al., 2012; Long et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Causier et al., 2012 and Long et al., 2006

claim: ABA, jasmonate and ethylene have been implicated in promoting senescence
source: These hormones were chosen because they have been implicated in promoting (ABA, jasmonate and ethylene) or preventing (cytokinin) senescence (Kim et al., 2015; Pré et al., 2008; Buchanan-Wollaston, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015, Pré et al., 2008, and Buchanan-Wollaston, 1996

claim: Cytokinin has been implicated in preventing senescence
source: These hormones were chosen because they have been implicated in promoting (ABA, jasmonate and ethylene) or preventing (cytokinin) senescence (Kim et al., 2015; Pré et al., 2008; Buchanan-Wollaston, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015, Pré et al., 2008, and Buchanan-Wollaston, 1996

claim: At2g17820/HK1 is a gene encoding a receptor that mediates ABA, drought and salt stress responses
source: In addition to the ABA catabolic enzyme gene, CYP707A2, induction of ABIG1 also regulates At2g17820/HK1, a gene encoding a receptor that mediates ABA, drought and salt stress responses (Wollbach et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wollbach et al., 2008

claim: ABIG1 induction regulates the gene encoding the ethylene receptor ERS2
source: induction of ABIG1 also regulates At2g17820/HK1, a gene encoding a receptor that mediates ABA, drought and salt stress responses (Wollbach et al., 2008) and the gene encoding the ethylene receptor ERS2.
evidence: Identified in RNA-seq analysis of ABIG1 induction

claim: Two transcription factor genes in the jasmonate pathway, ORA59 and TIFY7, were down-regulated by ABIG1 induction
source: Finally, two transcription factor genes in the jasmonate pathway, ORA59 and TIFY7 were down-regulated in this experiment.
evidence: Identified in RNA-seq analysis

claim: ABIG1 promotes drought-induced senescence in part by changing the amount of ABA in the plant while also altering the sensitivity of the cell to ABA, ethylene and jasmonate
source: The identities of these regulated genes support a model in which ABIG1 promotes drought-induced senescence in part by changing the amount of ABA in the plant while also altering the sensitivity of the cell to ABA, ethylene and jasmonate.
evidence: Inferred from the identities of genes regulated by ABIG1

claim: SAG113/HAI1/AT5g59220 encodes a PP2C phosphatase homologous to those in the core ABA signaling pathway

source: In addition, ABIG1 transcript induction did not alter levels of AtNAP (AT1G69490; Zhang and Gan, 2012) , a known positive regulator of SAG113/HAI1 through which ABA is thought to act.

claim: ABA up-regulation of SAG113/HAI1 likely occurs through a parallel pathway to ABIG1

claim: Increases in cytokinin activity are associated with both drought tolerance and with inhibition of senescence
source: Alterations in cytokinin metabolism, particularly increases in cytokinin activity, are associated with both drought tolerance and with inhibition of senescence (Peleg et al., 2011; Kuppu et al., 2013).

claim: abig1-1 mutant seedlings have higher steady state levels of mRNA from the CYP735A2/At1G67110 cytokinin biosynthetic gene

claim: The change in CYP735A2 steady state values is likely an indirect effect of reduced ABIG1 action

claim: Elevated CYP735A2 mRNA levels decreased in the abig1 mutant in response to exogenous ABA

claim: Some ABA responses remain intact in abig1 mutants
source: Thus, not only do some ABA responses remain intact in abig1 mutants, the physiological and developmental context of the abig1 mutant also results in novel responses to ABA.

claim: The physiological and developmental context of the abig1 mutant results in novel responses to ABA
source: Thus, not only do some ABA responses remain intact in abig1 mutants, the physiological and developmental context of the abig1 mutant also results in novel responses to ABA.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response of CYP735A2 to ABA in mutant vs wild-type

claim: ABIG1/HAT22 has similar regulation patterns to two other known ABA signaling genes, PYL6 and CIPK12

claim: Expression of ABIG1/HAT22 increases in response to exogenous ABA and drought

source: 6/ Induction of ABIG1/HAT22 regulates CYP707A3, a gene encoding an enzyme that mediates ABA breakdown.

claim: Abscisic acid was first discovered for its ability to promote organ abscission, a process known to be regulated by ethylene

source: Two ethylene receptors, ETR1 and ETR2, regulate the sensitivity of germination to ABA (Wilson et al., 2014)

source: Absicisic acid biosynthetic enzymes are required for ethylene signaling in the inhibition of rice root growth (Ma et al., 2014)

source: A screen for ABA insensitive mutants in Arabidopsis root growth resulted in the recovery of mutations in the ethylene signaling pathway as well as in the auxin signaling pathway (Thole et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thole et al., 2014

claim: The central signaling kinase of the ethylene signaling pathway, CTR1, mediates both ABA and ethylene signaling in the moss Physcomitrellum
source: The link between ABA signaling and ethylene signaling appears to be ancient as the central signaling kinase of the ethylene signaling pathway, CTR1, mediates both ABA and ethylene signaling in the moss Physcomitrellum (Yasumura et al., 2015).

claim: Reduced growth in ABA biosynthesis mutants and in response to exogenous ABA have both been shown to be mediated in part through the ethylene pathway

claim: Loss of function in a step of a biosynthetic pathway may cause accumulation of precursors and/or increased flow through side branches of the biosynthetic pathway
source: For another, loss of function in a step of a biosynthetic pathway may cause accumulation of precursors and/or increased flow through side branches of the biosynthetic pathway.

claim: An earlier step in the ABA biosynthetic pathway shows accumulation of precursors or increased flow through side branches
source: The latter appears to be the case for an earlier step in the ABA biosynthetic pathway (Avendaño-Vázqueza, 2014) and for some mutants in the auxin biosynthesis pathway (Brumos et al., 2014).

source: Class II HD-ZIP proteins are transcription factors that have been shown to regulate shoot growth and development (Turchi et al., 2013; Park et al., 2013; Rice et al., 2014).

claim: Class II HD-ZIP proteins include a DNA binding homeodomain and a leucine zipper dimerization domain
source: They include a DNA binding homeodomain and a leucine zipper dimerization domain.

claim: Class II HD-ZIP proteins bind to a palindromic sequence as dimers
source: Class II HD-ZIP proteins bind to a palindromic sequence as dimers and in several cases have been shown to repress their own transcription (Ohgishi et al., 2001; Ciarbelli et al., 2008).

claim: Several members of the HD-ZIPII family include an EAR like domain which can interact with TOPLESS family co-repressors to mediate transcriptional inhibition

claim: Many of the genes within the HD-ZIPII family are regulated by one or both REVOLUTA and KANADI transcription factors
source: Many of the genes within the HD-ZIPII family of genes, like ABIG1/HAT22, are regulated by one or both REVOLUTA and KANADI transcription factors (Reinhart et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2014; Brandt et al., 2012).

claim: mRNA levels for several of the class II HD-ZIP genes are regulated by environmental and hormonal inputs, including ABA, auxin and red/far red light
source: In addition to regulation by developmental factors, mRNA levels for several of the class II HD-ZIP genes are also regulated by environmental and hormonal inputs, including ABA, auxin and red/far red light with the exact response to stimulus dependent on the particular Class II HD-ZIP gene in question (Ciarbelli et al., 2008).

claim: A general role for HD-ZIPII proteins is to link environmental and tissue specific signals to growth control

claim: ATHB17 and ATHB18 are the distantly related alpha type Class II HD-ZIP genes
source: Two of the ten Class II HD-ZIP genes in Arabidopsis are the distantly related alpha type Class II HD-ZIP genes ATHB17 and ATHB18.

source: Like ABIG1/HAT22, ATHB17 mRNA is also increased by ABA and by salt and drought stress (Park et al., 2013).

claim: ATHB17 activity inhibits growth
source: Also like ABIG1/HAT22, ATHB17 activity inhibits growth and athb17 mutant seedlings are resistant to ABA mediated growth inhibition.

claim: athb17 mutant seedlings are resistant to ABA mediated growth inhibition
source: Also like ABIG1/HAT22, ATHB17 activity inhibits growth and athb17 mutant seedlings are resistant to ABA mediated growth inhibition.
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2013

claim: athb17 loss of function mutant seedlings were more drought resistant
source: However, unlike the case for ABIG1/HAT22, athb17 loss of function mutant seedlings were more drought resistant and ATHB17 overexpressors were more drought sensitive.

claim: ATHB17 overexpressors were more drought sensitive
source: However, unlike the case for ABIG1/HAT22, athb17 loss of function mutant seedlings were more drought resistant and ATHB17 overexpressors were more drought sensitive.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with cited literature on ATHB17

claim: ATHB17 overexpressing plants led to greener, more chloroplast dense cells
source: Another difference between ABIG1/HAT22 and ATHB17 is that Hymus et al. (2013) found that ATHB17 overexpressing plants led to greener, more chloroplast dense cells while we find that overexpressing ABIG1/HAT22 causes leaves to be yellow and less green.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hymus et al., 2013

claim: Overexpressing ABIG1/HAT22 causes leaves to be yellow and less green
source: Another difference between ABIG1/HAT22 and ATHB17 is that Hymus et al. (2013) found that ATHB17 overexpressing plants led to greener, more chloroplast dense cells while we find that overexpressing ABIG1/HAT22 causes leaves to be yellow and less green.
evidence: Demonstrated in overexpression experiments in this study

claim: Transgenic maize lines overexpressing a truncated form of the Arabidopsis ATHB17 gene have been permitted for crop use by USDA
source: Recently, transgenic maize lines overexpressing a truncated form of the Arabidopsis ATHB17 gene, a type alpha class II HD-ZIP gene, lacking a presumed transcriptional repression domain and presumed to act as a dominant negative (Rice et al., 2014), have been permitted for crop use by USDA (Monsanto Petition (14-213-01p) for Determination of Non-regulated Status for Increased Ear Biomass MON 874Ø3 Maize.)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rice et al., 2014 and USDA petition

claim: The ATHB17 overexpressing maize plants are described as having greater ear biomass
source: In this application, the ATHB17 overexpressing plants are described as having greater ear biomass.
evidence: Based on description in USDA petition

claim: Drought has been shown to increase levels of the ABA biosynthetic enzyme, NCED9, in the parenchyma cells surrounding the xylem
source: Drought has been shown to increase levels of the ABA biosynthetic enzyme, NCED9, in the parenchyma cells surrounding the xylem (Endo et al. 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Endo et al., 2008

claim: Increased ABA in the vascular parenchyma acts through the ABI1 ABA co-receptor to increase ABIG1 mRNA levels
source: We propose that increased ABA in the vascular parenchyma acts through the ABI1 ABA co-receptor to increase ABIG1 mRNA levels.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental observations

source: Increased levels of ABIG1 transcription factor in turn regulate a suite of genes, through direct or indirect action, that includes those shown in Figure 6.

evidence: Inferred from the identities of regulated genes and observed phenotypes

claim: There are no ABRE elements upstream of the ABIG1 gene

evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: ABIG1 expression is strengthened and expanded in the vasculature in response to ABA
source: Nevertheless, Q-RTPCR analysis shows that regulation occurs within hours of ABA application and gene trap analysis shows that ABIG1 expression is strengthened and expanded in the vasculature in response to ABA.
evidence: Demonstrated by GUS reporter analysis

claim: Increased ABIG1 levels have profound consequences on the plant, resulting in growth inhibition and leaf yellowing
source: Our experiments also show that increased ABIG1 levels have profound consequences on the plant, resulting in growth inhibition and leaf yellowing.
evidence: Demonstrated by overexpression experiments

claim: ABIG1 can down-regulate a gene encoding an ABA catabolic enzyme
source: Furthermore, the finding that ABIG1 can down-regulate a gene encoding an ABA catabolic enzyme suggests that ABA can act to increase its own levels via a positive feedback loop that includes ABIG1/HAT22.

claim: ABA can act to increase its own levels via a positive feedback loop that includes ABIG1/HAT22
source: Furthermore, the finding that ABIG1 can down-regulate a gene encoding an ABA catabolic enzyme suggests that ABA can act to increase its own levels via a positive feedback loop that includes ABIG1/HAT22.
evidence: Inferred from the regulation of ABA catabolic enzyme by ABIG1

claim: ABIG1 participates in a parallel path in which ABA regulates growth and the decision to undergo senescence
source: We propose that ABIG1 participates in a parallel path in which ABA regulates growth and the decision to undergo senescence (Figure 7).

source: We note that an increase in ABA levels precedes an increase in ABIG1/HAT22 levels in maturing and senescing leaves as found in transcriptome inventories of developing Arabidopsis leaves (Breeze et al., 2011).

claim: In crop plants such as sorghum and rice, drought conditions often induce premature senescence
source: In crop plants such as sorghum and rice, drought conditions often induce premature senescence.
evidence: Established knowledge in crop science

claim: Varieties that resist drought-induced senescence are referred to as possessing a 'stay green' phenotype
source: Varieties that resist this induced senescence are referred to as possessing a 'stay green' phenotype (Thomas and Ougham, 2014).

source: Stay green traits from wild relatives have been incorporated into a variety of crop plants to breed drought resistant varieties.
evidence: Established practice in plant breeding

source: The abig1-1 mutant behaves like a stay green mutant in its ability to remain green and to maintain an upright shoot under drought conditions.
